content: Marasmus is a severe form of malnutrition that occurs when the body depletes its stores of subcutaneous fat and muscle due to the mobilization of all available energy and nutrients. This condition arises from a deficiency of both protein and energy-providing nutrients, such as carbohydrates and fats, in the diet. It is most commonly observed in children under the age of one year. Marasmus is prevalent in regions affected by famine, limited food availability, and low levels of education, where individuals may lack knowledge about proper dietary practices. It is more common in impoverished countries, particularly during periods of drought, natural disasters, or political instability, which disrupt food supplies and lead to widespread malnutrition. In the United States, marasmus is rare among children, with isolated cases often linked to severe neglect or child abuse. However, it is estimated that up to 50% of elderly individuals in nursing homes in the U.S. may not consume adequate protein in their diets. The clinical presentation of marasmus includes a range of symptoms. Affected individuals may appear emaciated, resembling an elderly man, with dry, peeling skin that does not change in color. There is significant loss of muscle mass, sunken eyes, and protruding cheeks. The area around the mouth may lose fullness, resulting in a monkey-like facial appearance. Unlike kwashiorkor, generalized swelling (edema) is typically absent in marasmus. Other symptoms include a sunken abdomen, chronic diarrhea, failure to gain weight or grow, fatigue, changes in hair color or texture, increased susceptibility to infections due to a weakened immune system, irritability, lethargy, dermatitis, and, in severe cases, shock. Late-stage findings may include coma and other life-threatening complications. Diagnosis of marasmus involves a thorough physical examination, which may reveal an enlarged liver (hepatomegaly) and other signs of malnutrition. Laboratory tests are often conducted to assess the patient’s overall health and nutritional status. These tests may include arterial blood gas analysis, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), complete blood count (CBC), creatinine clearance, serum creatinine, serum potassium, total protein levels, and urinalysis. Treatment for marasmus focuses on providing adequate calories and protein to correct the nutritional deficiencies. Early intervention is critical to achieving favorable outcomes. In cases of severe malnutrition, treatment begins with the administration of carbohydrates, simple sugars, and fats to provide energy. Protein is introduced gradually after the initial caloric needs are met. Vitamin and mineral supplementation is essential. Refeeding must be done cautiously, as the sudden introduction of high-calorie foods can lead to complications. Many malnourished children develop lactose intolerance and may require lactase enzyme supplements to tolerate milk products. Children who recover from marasmus may not reach their full potential for height and growth. The prognosis for marasmus depends on the timing of treatment. Early intervention generally leads to good outcomes, although permanent physical and mental impairments may occur in some cases. If left untreated or if treatment is delayed, marasmus can be life-threatening. Complications of marasmus include coma, permanent physical and mental disabilities, and shock. It is essential to seek medical attention if a child exhibits symptoms of marasmus. Prevention of marasmus involves ensuring a balanced diet that includes sufficient carbohydrates, fats (at least 10% of total caloric intake), and proteins (12% of total caloric intake). Alternative terms for marasmus include protein malnutrition, protein-calorie malnutrition, and malignant malnutrition.
